query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, phase stability is governed by a dynamic balance between the innate high configurational entropy (which kinetically suppresses phase separation) and a stress‐induced short‐range chemical ordering process (centered on Al-rich correlations) that is activated under compressive loading at elevated temperatures. This ordering transition subtly shifts the alloy from a fully disordered FCC state toward locally ordered (B2-like) regions, which in turn enhance high‐temperature strength, oxidation (environmental) resistance, and radiation tolerance through reduced diffusion and improved barrier effects, while the disordered state favors cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: Al0.1CrCoFeNi alloy in a relaxed state exhibiting a predominantly disordered FCC phase with inherent but modest Al–Al clustering.
generation.intervention: Impose a controlled compressive stress (versus a tensile or unstressed control) during thermal treatment at an elevated temperature (e.g., around 700 K) to trigger the ordering transition.
generation.conditions: Compare two sets of identically processed Al0.1CrCoFeNi samples—one subjected to compressive loading and one maintained under tensile or stress-free conditions—over a temperature range from 300 K to 1000 K while keeping composition, environment, and strain rate constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The extent of short-range chemical ordering, especially the amplification of Al–Al (and coupled Al–Ni) pair correlations transitioning into localized B2-like ordered domains.
generation.mechanism: Under compressive loading at moderate-to-high temperatures, local atomic rearrangements are energetically favored, deepening Al-rich clustering and initiating ordering transitions. This enhanced ordering reduces atomic mobility (sluggish diffusion effects), stabilizes ordered domains that act as barriers to defect migration, and reinforces protective oxide formation; consequently, high-temperature strength, oxidation resistance, and radiation tolerance improve, though these ordered regions may limit the ductility required for cryogenic toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples under compressive stress will show a measurable increase in short-range order (as evidenced by heightened Al–Al and Al–Ni pair correlations and emerging B2-like features) relative to the control. Correspondingly, these samples should exhibit increased high-temperature strength, lower oxidation rates (via more stable/passivating oxide scales), and improved resistance to irradiation-induced precipitation. In contrast, samples under tensile or stress-free conditions will maintain a disordered FCC structure that favors better cryogenic toughness.
generation.baseline: Al0.1CrCoFeNi samples processed without compressive stress (or under tensile loading) where high configurational entropy dominates, maintaining a predominantly disordered FCC phase with only modest, non-enhanced short-range clustering.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for low-to-moderate Al contents (e.g., Al mole fraction near 0.1) within the temperature window of approximately 300–1000 K and under moderate compressive strains. Extreme compositions, temperatures beyond this range, or very high strain rates might invoke additional phenomena not captured by this mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: While MD simulations (PMC4976365::web::000 and PMC4976365::web::012) have demonstrated a compressive-loading–induced clustering-to-ordering transition and ion irradiation studies (PMC4999872::web::014) show entropy-driven kinetic suppression of phase separation, no integrated experimental study has yet quantitatively linked stress-induced ordering to multi-environment performance metrics such as oxidation resistance and radiation tolerance. Therefore, extending the molecular-scale ordering observations to macroscopic performance effects introduces uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Al0.1CrCoFeNi HEA samples that are identical in composition and processing history. Subject one group to a controlled compressive loading regime at approximately 700 K, while the control group remains under tensile or negligible stress. After thermal treatment, employ high-resolution characterization (e.g., atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM) to quantify short-range ordering and phase fraction changes. Follow up with performance tests: high-temperature mechanical tests, oxidation (e.g., mass gain and oxide scale composition) experiments, and irradiation exposure coupled with defect density measurements.
measurements: Quantitative pair-correlation statistics (especially Al–Al and Al–Ni correlations) using atom probe/TEM
Phase composition and fraction (FCC vs. B2-like regions) via XRD/TEM
Oxidation rate and oxide scale integrity (via thermogravimetric analysis and microscopy)
Irradiation-induced defect density using TEM or positron annihilation spectroscopy
Cryogenic toughness via mechanical testing at low temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the compressive-loaded samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in local short-range ordering (i.e., similar pair-correlation profiles and phase fractions as in the control) and no concomitant improvements in high-temperature strength, oxidation resistance, or irradiation tolerance—and if cryogenic toughness does not inversely correlate as predicted—then the hypothesis that stress-induced ordering governs phase stability and the multi-environment performance is falsified.
